note: The UK is the best-sourced tradition in this table, because AHDB's Meat Purchasing Guide publishes a page per sub-cut and routinely puts the Latin name in the page title — `Feather – split and fully trimmed (Infraspinatus)`, `Main Topside Muscle (semimembranosus)`, `Clod Shin (Boneless) (Biceps Brachaii)`. That gives UK-native muscle attributions for the whole hind leg and most of the shoulder, without having to bridge through American cut names. Two things it does not give: rib numbers for anything except the fore rib, and any muscle name at all for thick rib, thin rib, brisket, shin or the head. Rib numbers appear in exactly two specs — the fore rib is 'ribs 7, 8, 9 and 10' and the sirloin is 'A 3-rib sirloin' — and the rest of the rib arithmetic here is derived from those two and graded `inferred`. Note also that AHDB serves the same guide from four hostnames — ahdb.org.uk, archive.ahdb.org.uk, horticulture.ahdb.org.uk, potatoes.ahdb.org.uk — with identical content; the URL cited is the one actually fetched.

cuts.dispute: How many wing ribs the sirloin carries is not settled even within AHDB. The Sirloin B004 spec says '2-rib bone sirloin'; the V005 standard-trim spec opens 'A 3-rib sirloin'; the atlas's own cut text says three. Since the fore rib is fixed at ribs 7-10 by the B001 spec, a three-rib sirloin begins at rib 11 and a two-rib sirloin at rib 12. Rib 11 is taken here as the outer bound, with the spread recorded rather than averaged away. The false-friend problem is exactly why the bound matters more than the name: `longissimus` alone cannot tell a British sirloin from an American one, and `from rib-11 to ilium` can — an American short loin would start at rib 13 and an American sirloin would not contain the longissimus as its defining muscle at all. Gluteus medius is listed as a trace only, on the strength of AHDB explicitly assigning the 'D' muscle to the rump; the CFIA contre-filet quote, which does list the gluteus, describes a Canadian cut whose line sits further back, and is cited here for the longissimus/multifidus pairing rather than for the gluteus.

cuts.dispute:
The UK skirt trio is the interesting case here, and only two thirds of it is settled.

THICK SKIRT: settled. It is the onglet, and the onglet is the crura. Scotch Beef PGI describes the thick skirt as an internal organ hanging below the heart off the diaphragm; Wikipedia's hanger-steak entry gives 'skirt (UK)' as a synonym and pins the anatomy to 'the crura, or legs, of the diaphragm … attached to the last rib and to the front of several of the lumbar vertebrae'. That is `diaphragm-crus`, and it agrees with the French onglet finding already in FINDINGS.md. So the British naming does NOT swap onglet and hampe, despite 'thick skirt' sounding as though it ought to mean the thicker costal sheet. FINDINGS.md's warning that UK 'thick skirt' muddies the onglet/hampe pair is about the name, not about the anatomy: the anatomy comes out the same as the French.

THIN SKIRT: settled, and settled by AHDB itself, whose page is titled with the Latin — 'Inside Skirt (Transversus Abdominis)'.

GOOSE SKIRT: not settled, and this is why the cut is graded contested. (a) The common trade answer is the rectus abdominis, the muscle Calkins calls simply 'Flank'. (b) Great British Chefs conflates it both with bavette and with thick flank — 'Bavette – also known as thick flank or goose skirt' — which cannot be right, since AHDB's own thick flank is the quadriceps in the hind leg while its bavette is Thin Flank B006 in the belly, and those are not the same muscle or the same quarter of the animal. (c) Some UK retail copy calls goose skirt part of the diaphragm, which would collide head-on with thick skirt. AHDB's own Goose Skirt page (Thin Flank B002) settles nothing: it says only that the cut is trimmed of gristle and fat, and names no muscle at all. (a) is taken as the entry, with (b) and (c) recorded rather than adopted.

A fourth point, which is an absence rather than a conflict: the costal diaphragm — the American outside skirt, the French hampe — has no distinct British name. AHDB's 'Skirt Steaks (diaphragm)' is filed under Offal B002 and trims the whole diaphragm as one item without separating the sheet from the crura. So the costal sheet is given entirely to `thin-rib` and does not appear here at all, even though its caudal edge does reach the flank — a `whole` has to be exclusive if these bounds are ever to carve geometry.

Bounds: inferred throughout. No UK spec gives a rib or vertebral boundary for the thin flank; the last rib is used as the cranial end because that is where the carcass is quartered.

cuts.dispute: That ox cheek is the masseter is not seriously disputed anywhere, but nothing fetched this pass states it in so many words. The Calkins table covers only the 32 carcass muscles ranked for tenderness and has no head rows at all; AHDB's guide stops at the carcass, and its offal pages do not reach the head table. Graded inferred rather than given a quote it does not have — the same call us.json makes for the American cheek.
